parents.course: Introduction to the Study of Literature and Culture

ns2:section.sectionText: This section of ENGL 200 will have two primary goals: (1) to familiarize you with the major forms and media you are likely to encounter as scholars of literature (primarily poetry, drama, prose, and film) and (2) to interrogate the value of the study of literature. As a concept for putting all of these varied forms and media in conversation with one another, we will focus on both canonical texts and works written in response to them or a tradition to which they belong. For example, we will read Lorraine Hansberry’s A Raisin in the Sun and Bruce Norris’ prequel/sequel Clybourne Park and examine how these texts speak to one another. We will read multiple poetic interpretations of the Greek myth of Leda and the Swan that span a century of literary and cultural thought. We will also read Joseph Moncure March’s 1928 poem The Wild Party and examine how cartoonist and graphic novelist Art Spiegelman’s 1994 illustrated edition of the poem influences how we make meaning from March’s words. Throughout the semester, we will consider the originals and their reimaginings. What do these new works add to our understandings of the original texts? What do they retain from the originals? What do they omit or revise? What do these revisions say about the cultural moment in which they were made? What value do the original texts retain after these interventions? We will use both our own close readings and the theories developed by various schools of critical thought to answer these questions. We will also put these works into conversation with articles and essays that articulate the value of the study of literature and the skills that we develop through this study. We will find concrete applications for these skills beyond the spaces of the classroom and academia. By the conclusion of the course, we will have not just developed skills for literary analysis, but articulate why and how these skills still matter.
